group.title: Time and daily life
group.blurb: The clock (including the half hour that runs backwards), days, months, seasons, the three time prepositions, and everything you say in a café.

topics.title: Telling the time
topics.summary: Dutch counts towards the next hour, so half vier is 3:30 and not 4:30. Once that clicks, the rest is quick.

items.en: What time does the class start?

items.nl: Weet u misschien hoe laat het is?
items.en: Do you perhaps know what time it is?

blocks.title: This is the one that catches everyone
blocks.body:
`half` in Dutch means **half way to** the next hour, not half past the current one.
- `half vier` = 3:30 (half way to four)
- `half negen` = 8:30
- `half een` = 12:30
So whenever you hear `half`, subtract one from the number you heard.

blocks.note: Between :20 and :40 Dutch counts from the half hour, not from the hour. That is why 3:25 is vijf voor half vier.

blocks.title: The escape hatch
blocks.body: In shops, stations and at work people also use the digital style: `drie uur dertig`, `vijftien uur dertig`, `negen uur vijfenveertig`. It is always understood, so use it while the half-hour system settles in.

blocks.note: The apostrophe-s is a leftover of an old word for des. Say it as one word: sochtends, savonds.

items.nl: Om acht uur 's ochtends begin ik met werken.
items.en: At eight in the morning I start work.

items.nl: Om acht uur kijken we altijd naar het nieuws op tv.
items.en: At eight o'clock we always watch the news on TV.

items.nl: 's Avonds lees ik meestal een boek.
items.en: In the evening I usually read a book.
items.note: fronted, so the verb comes second and ik follows

blocks.title: Dutch punctuality is real
blocks.body: An invitation for 11:00 means 11:00. If you will be more than five minutes late, a quick message is expected. `Sorry, ik ben iets later` covers it.

key_takeaways: half vier is 3:30, so subtract one from the number you hear after half.
Between :20 and :40 Dutch counts from the half hour: vijf voor half vier is 3:25.
kwart over and kwart voor work exactly like English quarters.
's ochtends, 's middags, 's avonds, 's nachts split the day.

exercises.prompt: What time is half vier?
exercises.explain: half counts towards the next hour, so half vier is half way to four: 3:30.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 8:30?
exercises.explain: 8:30 is half way to nine, so half negen.

exercises.prompt: Say 3:15 in Dutch.
exercises.explain: Quarters work like English: kwart over drie.

exercises.prompt: What time is vijf voor half vier?
exercises.explain: half vier is 3:30, and five before that is 3:25.

exercises.prompt: Say 3:45 in Dutch.
exercises.explain: Quarter to four is kwart voor vier.

exercises.prompt: Build: at eight o'clock we always watch the news.
exercises.explain: The time phrase is the first element, so the verb comes second and we follows it.

exercises.prompt: Which one means 'at night'?
exercises.explain: 's nachts is roughly midnight to six. 's avonds is the evening.

exercises.prompt: Ask what time the class starts.
exercises.explain: de les is third person singular, so stem plus t: begint.

topics.title: Days, months, seasons and time prepositions
topics.summary: The calendar vocabulary plus the three-way choice that decides everything: op for days, in for months and seasons, om for clock times.

blocks.note: Days and months are written in lower case in Dutch, unlike English. Only the start of a sentence gives them a capital.

blocks.title: morgen has two jobs
blocks.body: `morgen` on its own means **tomorrow**. Inside `goedemorgen` and `vanmorgen` it means **morning**. Context sorts it out: `Tot morgen!` is see you tomorrow, `vanmorgen` is this morning.

rows: Ik heb les om negen uur.
blocks.note: One way to remember it: om is the smallest unit (a point on the clock), op is a day, in is anything bigger.

blocks.title: Other useful ones
blocks.body:
- `van ... tot ...`: `De field trip is van 10:45 tot 14:00.`
- `'s maandags` means every Monday, a habit: `'s Maandags werk ik thuis.`
- `over`: `Ik kom over tien minuten.` (in ten minutes from now)
- `sinds`: `Ik woon hier sinds 2022.`
- `tijdens`: `tijdens de les`

blocks.title: Often no preposition at all
blocks.body: With a day used as the first element, Dutch usually drops the preposition altogether: `**Vrijdag** komt mijn moeder op bezoek.` Same with `volgende week`, `elke dag`, `vanavond`: `Volgende week ga ik naar Parijs.`

items.nl: Ik sport twee keer per week.
items.en: I do sport twice a week.

items.nl: Hij belt elke dag zijn moeder.
items.en: He calls his mother every day.

items.nl: Wij gaan altijd in de zomer naar Frankrijk.
items.en: We always go to France in the summer.
My date of birth is 15 August 1988.

blocks.title: jarig zijn
blocks.body: Dutch has a dedicated adjective for having a birthday: `Ik ben jarig.` (It is my birthday.) `Wanneer ben je jarig?` The person celebrating is `de jarige`, and the standard congratulation is `Gefeliciteerd!`

key_takeaways: Days and months are lower case in Dutch.
op for a day or date, in for a month, season or year, om for a clock time.
Fronting a day usually drops the preposition: Vrijdag komt mijn moeder.
's maandags means every Monday, as a habit.
jarig zijn is the verb for having a birthday.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ik ben jarig ___ januari.
exercises.explain: in goes with months, seasons and years.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ik heb les ___ maandag.
exercises.explain: op goes with a specific day or date.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ik heb les ___ negen uur.
exercises.explain: om goes with clock times.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Kerst is ___ de winter.
exercises.explain: Seasons take in: in de winter, in de zomer.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ik ben geboren ___ 1988.
exercises.explain: A specific year takes in.

exercises.prompt: Which is written correctly?
exercises.explain: Days take op and are written in lower case.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Tot morgen!' mean?
exercises.explain: morgen on its own is tomorrow. Inside vanmorgen and goedemorgen it means morning.

exercises.prompt: Build: he calls his mother every day.
exercises.explain: Subject, verb, then the time phrase before the object.

exercises.prompt: Say it is your birthday.
exercises.explain: jarig zijn is the fixed way to say you are having your birthday.

topics.title: At the café and talking about favourites
topics.subtitle_nl: in het café en over voorkeuren praten
topics.summary: Ordering, paying, splitting the bill, and the two different ways Dutch says favourite.

items.en: Could I have the menu, please?
I am having a beer now.

blocks.title: The little-word habit
blocks.body: Drinks almost always take the `-je` ending in a café: `een biertje`, `een wijntje`, `een kopje koffie`, `een glaasje water`. It is not about size, it is friendliness. Ordering `een bier` is not wrong, just blunter.

blocks.title: Never call out Ober!
blocks.body: Shouting `Ober!` across the room is what tourists do in films. In the Netherlands you catch the server's eye, raise a hand slightly, or wait to be noticed. If you must speak, `Sorry?` or `Mag ik even?` is plenty.

sections.heading: The whole exchange, start to finish

items.nl: Doe mij maar een spa rood.
items.en: I will have a sparkling water.

items.nl: Een pilsje, een cola en een spa rood. Alstublieft.
items.en: A beer, a cola and a sparkling water. Here you go.
Could I have the bill, please?

items.nl: Kan ik betalen? / Kan ik afrekenen?
Dat is 10 euro, alstublieft. Pinnen of contant?
items.en: That is 10 euros, please. Card or cash?

items.nl: Contant graag. Alstublieft, het is goed zo.
items.en: Cash please. Here you are, keep the change.

items.nl: Dank u wel. Fijne avond nog!
items.en: Thank you. Have a nice evening!

blocks.title: spa rood and spa blauw
blocks.body: Dutch cafés name water by bottle colour: `spa rood` is sparkling, `spa blauw` is still. `Een kraantje` or `een glaasje kraanwater` is tap water, though not every place serves it. A `pilsje` is a small draught lager, the default beer.

blocks.title: Two Dutch café habits
blocks.body: Most places are **card only**, so `Kan ik pinnen?` is the practical question and cash can be refused. Tipping is not obligatory: rounding up or leaving five to ten percent for good service is plenty, and `Laat maar zitten` handles it.

Dutch has two words for favourite and they behave differently.
- `lievelings-` is **glued onto the noun** as one word: `mijn lievelingseten`, `mijn lievelingsboek`, `mijn lievelingsfilm`, `mijn lievelingskleur`.
- `favoriete` is a **normal adjective** and takes the usual `-e`: `mijn favoriete vakantieland`, `mijn favoriete café`.

items.nl: Mijn lievelingseten is pasta met pesto.
items.en: My favourite food is pasta with pesto.
What is your favourite holiday country?
My favourite holiday country is Greece.

rows: liever is the comparative of graag
Most of all I drink coffee.
I do not care for fish.
blocks.note: graag, liever, liefst attach to the verb, not the noun. That is why they sit in the middle of the sentence.

blocks.title: lekker and leuk are not interchangeable
blocks.body: `lekker` is for taste, smell and physical comfort (`lekker eten`, `lekker weer`, `lekker slapen`). `leuk` is for things you enjoy (`een leuke film`, `een leuk feest`, `Wat leuk!`). Calling a film `lekker` says something else entirely.

items.nl: Wat drink je meestal in een café?
items.en: What do you usually drink in a café?

items.nl: Bestel jij al in het Nederlands?
items.en: Do you order in Dutch already?

items.nl: Hoe zeg je proost in jouw taal?
items.en: How do you say cheers in your language?
Do you ever buy a round?

items.nl: Geef je in jouw land altijd fooi?
items.en: Do you always tip in your country?

items.nl: Wat is jouw favoriete café in de buurt?
items.en: What is your favourite café around here?

key_takeaways: lievelings- is glued to the noun, favoriete is a normal adjective with -e.
Drinks take the -je form in a café: een biertje, een kopje koffie.
Kan ik pinnen? is the question that matters, since most places are card only.
graag, liever and het liefst go with the verb, in the middle of the sentence.
lekker is for taste and comfort, leuk is for things you enjoy.

exercises.prompt: Which is written correctly?
exercises.explain: lievelings- is glued onto the noun as one word.

exercises.prompt: Complete with favoriet: Mijn ___ vakantieland is Griekenland.
exercises.explain: favoriet is a normal adjective, and after mijn it takes -e.

exercises.prompt: Ask whether you can pay by card.
exercises.explain: pinnen is paying by debit card, and it is the standard question in a Dutch café.

exercises.prompt: The waiter asks Samen of apart? What is being asked?
options: Do you want to sit together?
exercises.explain: It is about the bill: one payment or one per person.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is natural Dutch?
options: Die film is lekker leuk gezellig.
exercises.explain: leuk is for things you enjoy. lekker is for taste, smell and physical comfort.

exercises.prompt: Build: I prefer to drink tea.
exercises.explain: liever goes with the verb, so it sits between the verb and the object.

exercises.prompt: Start with Dit rondje: this round is on me.
exercises.explain: The fronted object puts the emphasis on this round, so the subject moves behind the verb.

exercises.prompt: Ask whether the seat is free.
exercises.explain: Is deze plaats vrij? is the standard way to ask before sitting down.

exercises.prompt: You want to get the server's attention in a Dutch café. What do you do?
options: Catch their eye or raise a hand slightly
Stand up and walk to the kitchen
exercises.explain: Shouting Ober! is not done here. Eye contact or a small raised hand is the norm.

exercises.prompt: Ask whether your group may order.
exercises.explain: Mogen we bestellen? The second verb keeps its base form at the end.

exercises.prompt: The server asks Pinnen of contant? What is the choice?
exercises.explain: pinnen is paying by card, contant is cash. Many places take card only.

exercises.prompt: You want sparkling water. What do you order?
exercises.explain: Red is sparkling, blue is still. A kraantje is tap water and a pilsje is a beer.

exercises.explain: Het is goed zo is the usual way to round up and leave the rest.

topics.title: Making plans and reacting
topics.summary: How to suggest something with zullen, three other ways to invite someone, and a full set of yes and no answers that do not sound rude.

blocks.body:
`zullen` is the suggestion verb. It follows the two-verb pattern, so the second verb drops to the end.
- `Zal ik ...?` offers something **you** will do.
- `Zullen we ...?` proposes something you do **together**.

blocks.note: In a suggestion you almost only ever need zal ik and zullen we, so those two are worth drilling until they are automatic.

items.nl: Zal ik donderdag voor je koken?
items.en: Shall I cook for you on Thursday?

items.nl: Zal ik mijn naam even voor je spellen?
items.en: Shall I spell my name for you?
Shall we go shopping together tomorrow?
Shall we go to the cinema?
items.note: gaan is left out because it is obvious

rows: Ga je mee naar de dierentuin?
Are you coming to the zoo?
Do you want to come for a walk?
Heb je zin om ... te + base form
Heb je zin om morgen te zwemmen?
Do you fancy going swimming tomorrow?
blocks.note: Watch the split: zin in takes a noun, zin om ... te takes a verb. Mixing them up is the most common slip here.

items.en: What time shall we agree on?

items.nl: Zullen we om acht uur afspreken?
Ik zet het in mijn agenda.
items.en: I will put it in my diary.

blocks.title: gezellig
blocks.body: `gezellig` has no clean English match. It covers cosy, sociable and warm all at once, and it is the single most Dutch way to accept an invitation. `Ja, gezellig!` works for almost anything social.

rows: Nee, dan heb ik helaas geen tijd.
No, I have no time then.
Nee, ik heb dan al een afspraak.
No, I already have plans then.
Nee sorry, daar heb ik geen zin in.
No sorry, I do not feel like it.
Nee, dat vind ik niet zo leuk.
No, I do not really enjoy that.
Nee, ik hou niet van musea.
No, I do not like museums.
blocks.note: An availability reason is the easy no. A preference reason is direct, which Dutch people are comfortable with, but soften it with sorry and niet zo.

blocks.title: daar ... in
blocks.body:
`Daar heb ik geen zin in` looks scrambled because `daarin` splits around the rest of the sentence. The pattern is common:
- `Ik heb geen zin **in** koffie.` becomes `**Daar** heb ik geen zin **in**.`
- `Ik hou **van** koken.` becomes `**Daar** hou ik **van**.`
The `daar` fronts and the preposition stays at the end.

sections.heading: How is it going, on a scale

blocks.note: You can front the whole answer with Met mij gaat het ... , then finish with en met jou? Leaving off the return question sounds uninterested.

items.nl: Met mij gaat het prima, en met jou?
items.en: I am doing fine, and you?

items.nl: Het gaat wel, ik ben een beetje moe.
items.en: So-so, I am a bit tired.

sections.heading: Why everything goes in the diary

blocks.body:
In the Netherlands an `afspraak` is made for far more than English speakers expect. Turning up unannounced, even at a good friend's house, is unusual. Expect to plan:
- coffee with a colleague
- a drink with a friend
- dinner at someone's home
- a birthday visit
- the doctor, the hairdresser, the bank
Invitations often land a week or more ahead, and `Ik moet even in mijn agenda kijken` is a completely normal, non-evasive answer.

key_takeaways: Zal ik ...? offers what you will do, Zullen we ...? proposes something together.
zin in takes a noun, zin om ... te takes a verb.
Ja, gezellig! accepts almost any social invitation.
Turning something down on availability is easier than on preference.
In daar heb ik geen zin in, daar fronts and the preposition stays at the end.
Almost everything social is arranged by appointment, often a week ahead.

exercises.prompt: Build: shall we go shopping together tomorrow?
exercises.explain: zullen is conjugated in first position for a question, and winkelen drops to the end.

exercises.prompt: Offer to cook for someone on Thursday: ___ ik donderdag voor je koken?
exercises.explain: Zal ik ...? offers something you will do yourself.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Heb je zin om te zwemmen?
exercises.explain: A verb needs zin om ... te. zin in only takes a noun, as in zin in koffie.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Heb je zin ___ koffie?
exercises.explain: koffie is a noun, so it takes zin in.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks Zullen we zaterdag naar de markt? You are busy. Which fits best?
options: Nee, ik hou niet van jou.
exercises.explain: Turning something down on availability is the easy, polite no.

exercises.prompt: Build the reply: no sorry, I do not feel like that.
exercises.explain: daar fronts the sentence and the preposition in stays at the very end.

exercises.prompt: Which answer to Hoe gaat het? means 'so-so'?
exercises.explain: Het gaat wel sits in the middle of the scale: not bad, not great.

exercises.prompt: Accept an invitation in the most Dutch way possible.
exercises.explain: Ja, gezellig! is the classic acceptance. Leuk, prima and goed plan all work too.

exercises.prompt: A Dutch friend says Ik moet even in mijn agenda kijken. What does that signal?
options: they are genuinely checking their diary
exercises.explain: Diaries are taken seriously here. It is a literal answer, not a brush-off.

exercises.prompt: Build: are you coming along for a walk?
exercises.explain: meegaan splits, so mee sits in the middle and the second verb wandelen closes the sentence.
